name: Ash
lede: Ash is the pale grey of what is left after burning, a color that old writers treated as colorless, that dyers and bleachers used as an alkali, and that painters borrowed as a name for weak pigments.

sections.title: A word for what is left
sections.body:
*Ash* is the color of what remains after burning, and English has a family of words for it [1]. Paterson lists *ash-coloured* as whitish grey or brownish grey, *ashen* as grey and also as a very pale complexion, and *ashy* as simply grey [1]. A *cinereous* bird is ash grey, and *favillous* means the color of hot ash [1]. *Ashes of roses* is a pinkish grey and *ash-blond* a light blond, while *cendre*, the French word, means ash-coloured [1]. Paterson's entry for grey ties it to lead, to ash and to the hair of middle age [1].

The color is a pale, quiet grey, but it is not one fixed grey. Paterson's entries run from whitish and brownish grey to pinkish grey [1], and the swatch on this page is a pale greenish grey, found in the ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary as block 154 [2]. For the larger family see [[grey]], and for the nearest named neighbors [[cinereous]] and [[pale-grey]].

sections.title: Werner's ash grey
sections.body:
The oldest chart in our library to carry the name is Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, which Syme edited in 1821 [2]. Werner lists ash grey among his greys, as number 9, and gives three natural examples [2]. For the animal kingdom it is the breast of a long-tailed hen titmouse, for the vegetable kingdom fresh wood ashes, and for the mineral kingdom flint [2]. So the color name and its material share a source. Baty's book lists ash-grey among the grey names, beside lead-grey, pearl-grey, smoke-grey and steel-grey [3].

Werner's ash grey is paler and warmer than the swatch. The aged plate in our data reads as about #CBC8B7, a faint yellowish grey [2]. The swatch used here, #B2BEB5, is a good match for the ISCC-NBS block, "light greenish gray", at a color distance of 2.0 [2]. Both are approximate, because the first comes from the scan of an old plate and the second from a modern screen [2].

sections.title: The residue that goes white
sections.body:
Ancient writers treated ash as colorless. Aristotle, whom Birren quotes, held that the earth is naturally white and takes its hues from the moisture that tinges it, and he offered ash as proof: ashes turn white when the moisture is burned out of them [4]. Jarman's chapter on shadow quotes the same argument [15].

The alchemists found a use for the in-between. The fourteenth-century treatise of Simeon of Cologne, which Gage quotes, lists the colors a metal passes through during transmutation, and between true white and true red it places a certain ash-grey color that is not to be despised [13]. It is a minor stage in a long sequence, but it shows how ash grey was filed: not a color to aim for, but one that mattered on the way to something else [13].

sections.title: Cloth, mourning and a queen
sections.body:
Ash lent its name to clothing. Pastoureau argues that the toga that Romans wore for funerals was probably closer to an ash grey than to true black [5]. The Latin adjective for it, *pullus*, generally refers to a dark, drab wool that falls somewhere between grey and brown [5].

A better-documented case is Elizabeth I. As a young woman she wore red and crimson, but after she took the throne in 1558 she dressed mostly in white, black and gold, with subdued colors such as peach, ash and tawny [8]. St Clair says that scarlet would not do for a virgin queen after her coronation, so she turned to neutral or broken tones such as tawny, gold and ash [8].

sections.title: Ash in the vat and the laundry
sections.body:
Where ash really mattered was as an alkali. Wood ash steeped in water gives a lye, and lye cleaned cloth, made soap and set dye vats. Soap was made for centuries by the same recipe, wood ash with animal or vegetable fat, until potash and soda replaced the ash [6]. Three hundred years ago, linen bleachers around Glasgow spread cloth on bleaching greens and treated it with sour milk and fern ashes [7]. Pastoureau adds that washing with ash, clay or minerals could not make a pure white. It left whites with a bluish, greenish or greyish cast, which is why people in antiquity and the Middle Ages seldom wore truly white clothes [6].

The indigo vat needed the same alkali. Balfour-Paul says that dyers in many cultures made their vats alkaline with ash water or stale urine [9]. In the fourteenth century Genoese merchants shipped woad, and ash for the vats, to England's south coast, where they traded it for wool [9]. One writer on indigo vats whom Balfour-Paul cites preferred wood ash to lime, noting that even ash from wood of different ages behaves differently [9]. The Lombok villagers whom Finlay met mixed their indigo with ash to make it alkaline [10]. In vats on several continents, then, the grey powder was the unseen half of the process.

Ash also played a smaller part in yellow. Pastoureau notes that Germanic dyers, whom Roman writers disdained, made their yellows from broom, gorse, nettle, fern and the leaves of ash trees, which is the tree and not the residue [17].

sections.title: A glaze from the fire
sections.body: Celadon's soft green glaze, the best-known case of ash as an ingredient, is made of wood ash and kaolin, and Finlay stresses that all of it comes from the mountains and their forests [11]. The wood was also the fuel for the kiln, and its ash became part of the glaze [11]. The result is the color of [[celadon]], an ash-born green. Bone has a similar history: the white pigment came from bones heaped on open fires and burned until nothing but ash remained, a method with Neolithic evidence [15]. St Clair adds that prehistoric people also took a deep black from the ashes of their fires [16].

sections.title: Ashes as a pigment name
sections.body:
Painters used *ashes* as a trade name for pale, low-grade colors. In making ultramarine, Cennino Cennini had the lapis kneaded in lye several times; the first kneadings gave the best blue, and the last gave a greyer, paler product known as ultramarine ash [12]. Ball explains that this was used for pale blue oil glazes [12]. Cennino even describes the stone itself as "mixed like ashes", and says the less of that ash color it contains, the better [12].

The label spread to copper pigments. Blue verditer, a synthetic version of azurite, was known in France as *cendres bleus*, blue ashes [12]. Azurite was also listed under the old name blue ashes of Seville [14]. Hoogstraten, the Dutch painter, complained in the 1670s that "ashes" were not durable enough as a green [12], and de Mayerne's recipe for the far distance in a landscape called for the most beautiful ashes of ultramarine and white [13]. A passage on painting by candlelight that Gage quotes says the ash pigments, described as green or blue, look an extremely beautiful blue [13]. In the Pigment Compendium, "ashes of lead" is an old name for grey lead oxide [14]. Cennino's warning that over-ground malachite turns dingy and ashy belongs to the same vocabulary [10]. See [[malachite]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Ash is a fairly common color in our painting archive. About 2.16 per cent of the 23,781 paintings (513 of them) contain it, as photographed, and it is more common than 79 per cent of the named colors [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays the light, in 58 per cent of the 375 paintings where the within-painting test finds it [2].

It peaks in the 1900s: 2.4 per cent of the 1,674 paintings we have from that century (41 paintings), or 1.7 times the baseline of the same museums [2]. The painter most devoted to it is [[painter:paul-signac|Signac]], with 4 of his 18 works here, at 5.6 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [2]. Ash keeps company with Pale Turtle Green and Cement Grey more than chance would predict [2].

The earliest match is a painting of 1279, but that is a floor and not a first [2]. The archive's early centuries are thin, and the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, 542 years before the name's first record in our sources [2]. In printed English the word peaks in the 1920s, but this counts every sense of *ash*, the tree and the residue included, so it is not a measure of the color [2].
